subtopic_detail: Red swollen foreskin with dysuria in an uncircumcised boy
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 4 year old uncircumcised boy brought in by his father with a sore penis for two days. He has been crying when he passes urine and holding on, and his father noticed the end of the penis looks red and puffy.

His father has been retracting the foreskin daily at bath time because he read it should be pulled back to keep it clean. On examination the distal foreskin and glans are erythematous and oedematous with a small amount of thick discharge at the preputial opening. The foreskin is not retracted and returns easily to its resting position when you release it. He is passing urine in a normal stream and the abdomen is soft with no loin tenderness. He is afebrile and drinking normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 96/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Erythema and oedema of the distal prepuce and glans, thick discharge at the preputial opening, foreskin lies in normal position and is not trapped behind the glans, no cellulitis of the shaft, no inguinal lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise saline bathing with topical treatment and stop the daily forcible retraction of the foreskin
options.rationale: Localised balanoposthitis in an afebrile boy with a normal urinary stream is treated with saline baths and a topical agent, and the forced retraction that caused the microtrauma is stopped. Physiological adhesions separate on their own and forcible retraction is the usual precipitant. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Attempt manual reduction of the foreskin now with ice and sustained compression of the glans
options.rationale: Reduction manoeuvres treat paraphimosis, in which a retracted foreskin traps behind the corona and constricts the glans. This foreskin sits in its normal position and returns freely, so there is nothing to reduce. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Collect a clean catch urine sample and commence oral trimethoprim for a urinary tract infection
options.rationale: Urinary infection is suggested by fever, systemic upset, loin tenderness or an abnormal stream, none of which are present, and local inflammation readily explains the pain on voiding. Contamination from the inflamed prepuce also makes a sample unreliable at this moment. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Refer for circumcision to prevent recurrent episodes and to allow easier hygiene in the future
options.rationale: Circumcision is considered for recurrent balanoposthitis or for pathological scarring of the prepuce, not for a first uncomplicated episode. Most boys have no further trouble once retraction stops and the physiological adhesions are left alone. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

options.text: Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin because of the risk of ascending infection of the urinary tract
options.rationale: Parenteral antibiotics are for a child who is febrile or systemically unwell or who has spreading cellulitis of the shaft. An afebrile boy with localised preputial inflammation is managed at home with local measures. (Source: RCH CPG: Balanitis and balanoposthitis)

explanation.summary: Balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans and prepuce and is common in uncircumcised boys, frequently precipitated by forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin. Presentation is with local redness, swelling, discharge and pain on voiding, and the child is usually afebrile and systemically well. The essential differential is paraphimosis, where a retracted foreskin has become trapped behind the corona and constricts the glans, which is a urological emergency requiring reduction. Treatment of uncomplicated balanoposthitis is saline bathing and a topical agent, together with the crucial advice to stop forcible retraction, since the prepuce separates spontaneously over childhood. Systemic antibiotics and referral are reserved for spreading cellulitis, systemic illness, or recurrent disease with pathological scarring.
key_points: Forcible retraction of a physiologically adherent foreskin is the usual precipitant
Paraphimosis is the emergency mimic and is identified by a foreskin trapped behind the corona
Saline bathing plus a topical agent treats most first episodes at home
Fever, systemic upset or spreading cellulitis moves treatment to systemic antibiotics
Circumcision is for recurrent disease or pathological scarring, not a single episode
explanation.pearls: Distinguish physiological non retractility, which is normal in most boys until well into school age, from true pathological phimosis with a pale scarred fibrous ring at the tip, because only the latter is an indication for topical corticosteroid or surgical referral.

subtopic_detail: Crops of umbilicated papules with surrounding dermatitis in a school aged child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6 year old girl whose mother has noticed small bumps spreading across her daughter's trunk and armpit over three months. Two of them have become red and itchy in the past week and the mother is worried the school will exclude her.

There are around twenty firm dome shaped papules 2 to 4 mm across, several with a central dimple, clustered in the right axilla and scattered on the adjacent trunk. Two lesions are surrounded by a patch of dry itchy dermatitis. There is no honey coloured crust, no pustule, no surrounding warmth and no lymphadenopathy. She has mild atopic dermatitis controlled with an emollient and swims twice weekly at the local pool. She is otherwise well and fully immunised.

data_table.Examination: Approximately twenty firm umbilicated papules 2 to 4 mm on right axilla and trunk, two with surrounding eczematous change, no crusting or pustulation, no regional lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange immunological assessment including lymphocyte subsets given the number of lesions present
options.rationale: Immune workup is considered for very extensive or unusually persistent disease, especially with other infections or failure to thrive. Around twenty lesions over three months in a thriving child with mild atopic dermatitis is ordinary. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Explain that the lesions resolve without treatment and treat the surrounding dermatitis topically
options.rationale: Molluscum contagiosum in a well immunocompetent child is self limiting over months to a couple of years, and no exclusion from school or swimming is required. The itchy eczematous halo around individual lesions responds to a topical corticosteroid and emollient, which also reduces scratching and spread. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days to treat secondary bacterial infection of the lesions
options.rationale: Bacterial superinfection is suggested by honey coloured crust, pustulation, warmth and tenderness rather than by a dry itchy halo. The inflammation described is eczematous and antibiotics would not address it. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Refer for cryotherapy to all lesions and exclude her from swimming until the skin has cleared
options.rationale: Physical destruction is painful, risks scarring and dyspigmentation, and is generally avoided in young children given spontaneous resolution. Exclusion from school and swimming is not recommended and adds social cost without controlling transmission. (Source: RCH CPG: Molluscum contagiosum)

options.text: Prescribe topical permethrin to the whole body and treat all household contacts on the same day
options.rationale: Scabies is treated this way and presents with intensely itchy burrows in web spaces, wrists and axillae with affected household members, not with discrete umbilicated papules. The morphology described does not fit a mite infestation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

explanation.summary: Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection producing firm dome shaped umbilicated papules, most often in preschool and primary school children and frequently spread by direct contact and shared towels. Lesions are self limiting, usually clearing over six to eighteen months, and treatment is not required in immunocompetent children. Two phenomena worry families unnecessarily: an eczematous halo around lesions, which is an immune response and is treated with a topical corticosteroid, and the so called beginning of the end inflammation, in which lesions become red and angry shortly before resolving. Children are not excluded from school or swimming, though covering lesions and avoiding shared towels is sensible. Destructive treatments are painful and risk scarring and are reserved for selected situations.
key_points: Central umbilication of firm dome shaped papules is the diagnostic morphology
Spontaneous resolution over six to eighteen months is the natural history
An eczematous halo is an immune reaction and is treated with topical corticosteroid
No exclusion from school or swimming; cover lesions and avoid sharing towels
Very extensive or persistent disease prompts consideration of underlying immunodeficiency
explanation.pearls: Warn parents in advance that individual lesions often turn red, swollen and tender in the weeks before they disappear, because this beginning of the end reaction is regularly mistaken for bacterial infection and leads to unnecessary courses of oral antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Parental concern about inward pointing feet in a walking toddler
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 2 year old boy whose grandmother insists his feet point inwards and that he needs special boots. His parents say he trips a little more than his older sister did but plays happily at the park all afternoon.

He walks with both feet turned inwards to a similar degree and runs without difficulty. With him lying prone and the knees flexed, the foot points inwards relative to the thigh on both sides. Passive hip rotation is symmetrical with internal rotation of about 50 degrees and external rotation of about 45 degrees on each side. The lateral border of each foot is straight and there is no crease at the midfoot. There is no pain, no limp and no asymmetry, and he has met all developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical bilateral in-toeing gait, thigh foot angle inwardly directed and equal bilaterally, hip internal rotation 50 degrees and external rotation 45 degrees bilaterally, straight lateral foot borders, no pain or limp, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot
options.rationale: Serial casting treats metatarsus adductus, in which the forefoot deviates inwards giving a curved lateral border and a medial midfoot crease, and only when it is rigid. The foot borders are straight here so the deformity is not in the foot. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Arrange physiotherapy for a supervised programme of hip external rotation strengthening exercises
options.rationale: Rotational alignment of the tibia is determined by bone shape rather than muscle balance, so strengthening does not change it. Physiotherapy has a role where there is genuine neuromuscular abnormality, which the normal examination excludes. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Reassure the family that the gait corrects with growth and review if pain or asymmetry develops
options.rationale: Symmetrical in-toeing from internal tibial torsion in a painless child with symmetrical hip rotation and straight foot borders is a normal stage of lower limb development that remodels through early childhood. Referral is triggered by pain, asymmetry, limp, regression of gait or an abnormal neurological examination. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Prescribe corrective boots with a torsion bar to be worn overnight until the gait has normalised
options.rationale: Night braces and torsion bars do not alter the natural history and burden the child and family with equipment. They persist in family lore because spontaneous remodelling occurs regardless of what is worn. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

options.text: Arrange radiographs of both hips and lower limbs to measure the degree of femoral anteversion
options.rationale: Imaging is not used to assess rotational profile in a well child, since the diagnosis is made from the prone rotational examination at the bedside. Excess femoral anteversion also gives internal rotation far exceeding external rotation, which is not the pattern here. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing and out-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing has three levels of origin and the prone rotational examination localises which one applies. Metatarsus adductus lies in the foot and gives a curved lateral border with a medial midfoot crease, internal tibial torsion lies in the leg and gives an inwardly directed thigh foot angle, and excess femoral anteversion lies in the hip and gives internal rotation greatly exceeding external rotation with a W sitting preference. Internal tibial torsion typically appears when walking begins and remodels through the preschool years, while femoral anteversion peaks around age five and also improves. Reassurance is the treatment, since braces, special footwear and exercises do not change the natural history. Referral is prompted by pain, asymmetry, limp, functional limitation, deterioration or neurological abnormality.
key_points: Prone rotational examination localises in-toeing to foot, tibia or femur
Straight lateral foot border excludes metatarsus adductus as the cause
Symmetrical hip rotation argues against excess femoral anteversion
Internal tibial torsion appears with early walking and remodels spontaneously
Pain, asymmetry, limp or neurological signs are the referral triggers
explanation.pearls: Asymmetrical in-toeing deserves a different level of attention from symmetrical in-toeing, because unilateral rotational change with a subtle limp can be the presenting sign of a spastic hemiplegia or of hip pathology, and both are missed if the finding is filed as normal variation.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear after a low energy twist with normal initial radiographs
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 20 month old boy who has refused to walk since yesterday afternoon. His mother watched him catch his foot at the bottom of the slide at daycare and twist as he came off, and he cried for a few minutes then went back to playing before refusing to stand at bath time.

He crawls readily and cries when you attempt to stand him. There is no bruising or swelling of the leg. He is not tender over the hip, knee or ankle, but he withdraws consistently when you gently rotate the mid tibia between your palms. The right calf is not warm and the skin is intact. He has been afebrile at home, is eating normally and has no rash. Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the tibia and fibula reported by the radiologist show no fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, full painless passive range at hip, knee and ankle, no joint effusion, no bruising or swelling, pain on gentle torsion of the mid tibia, skin intact, calf normal temperature
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), anteroposterior and lateral tibia and fibula radiographs reported as no fracture identified

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent hip ultrasound and joint aspiration for suspected septic arthritis of the affected limb
options.rationale: Septic arthritis presents with fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain through passive hip movement, and this child is afebrile with a normal C-reactive protein and painless hip movement. Aspiration is invasive and the clinical picture points to bone rather than joint. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)

options.text: Refer to child protection services for a skeletal survey given a fracture with negative radiographs
options.rationale: The mechanism was witnessed, is developmentally plausible for a walking toddler and matches the injury pattern, so this is not an unexplained fracture. Concern would rise sharply if the same injury were found in a child not yet walking. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

options.text: Arrange a technetium bone scan on the same day to identify the site of the occult bony injury
options.rationale: Bone scanning is sensitive but delivers a significant radiation dose and is reserved for a limping child in whom the site of pathology genuinely cannot be localised. Here the pain localises to the tibia and empirical immobilisation achieves the same end. (Source: RCH CPG: Acutely limping child)

options.text: Immobilise the leg in an above knee backslab and arrange orthopaedic outpatient review in one week
options.rationale: An undisplaced spiral fracture of the tibial shaft in a toddler is frequently invisible on initial films and is a clinical diagnosis based on refusal to weight bear with focal pain on tibial torsion after a low energy twist. Immobilisation and review is standard, and repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction if confirmation is needed. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and reassurance since the radiographs have excluded a bony injury
options.rationale: Initial radiographs miss a substantial proportion of these fractures because the spiral lucency is undisplaced and may be visible in only one plane. Treating a normal film as an exclusion sends home a child with a genuine fracture and no protection. (Source: RCH CPG: Toddler fracture)

explanation.summary: The toddler fracture is an undisplaced spiral or oblique fracture of the tibial shaft in a child roughly between nine months and three years, produced by a low energy twisting force with the foot fixed. The classic trap is that initial radiographs are normal or show only a subtle lucency in one plane, so a negative film does not exclude the injury and the diagnosis rests on the history and on focal pain reproduced by gentle torsion of the tibia. Management is immobilisation with orthopaedic review, and periosteal reaction on films at one to two weeks confirms the diagnosis retrospectively when needed. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis are the important alternatives and are suggested by fever, systemic upset, raised inflammatory markers and pain on passive joint movement. A fracture of this kind in a child who is not yet independently mobile carries an entirely different significance and requires child protection assessment.
key_points: Low energy twist with a fixed foot in a toddler is the classic mechanism
Normal initial radiographs do not exclude the fracture; up to a third are occult
Focal pain on gentle tibial torsion with painless joint movement localises to bone
Immobilise and review; repeat films at one to two weeks show periosteal reaction
The same fracture in a pre-ambulant infant demands child protection assessment
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the child has been walking independently before accepting a toddler fracture as innocent, because a spiral tibial fracture in a child who has never cruised or walked has no plausible self generated mechanism and moves the presentation directly into a child protection pathway.

subtopic_detail: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete with night pain and a thigh mass
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 13 year old boy who plays basketball four times a week and has had pain at the front of his right knee for ten weeks. He was told at a previous visit that this was growing pain from sport and advised to rest, but he says it has worsened despite six weeks away from training.

He now wakes at night with the pain and has been taking paracetamol most nights. There is fullness over the lower thigh above the kneecap with a firm deep swelling that does not move with the quadriceps, and he is tender there rather than over the bony bump below the kneecap. The knee has a small effusion and full range of movement. He has lost 3 kg since his last recorded weight four months ago. He is afebrile and there is no history of trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Firm deep swelling over the distal femur with local tenderness, tibial tuberosity not tender, small knee effusion, full range of movement, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (130-170), white cell count 7.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5), alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (adolescent male 100-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise a graded quadriceps loading programme with activity modification and review in eight weeks
options.rationale: This is the management of traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity, where tenderness sits over the bony prominence below the kneecap and pain settles with relative rest. Tenderness above the kneecap and deterioration despite six weeks off sport contradict that diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Arrange a knee magnetic resonance scan as the initial imaging investigation for the effusion
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is essential for local staging but follows the plain radiograph, which characterises the aggressive periosteal reaction and matrix that establish suspicion. Ordering a scan limited to the knee also risks missing a lesion centred in the femoral metaphysis. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Start empirical oral antibiotics for subacute osteomyelitis and review the response in one week
options.rationale: Subacute osteomyelitis can mimic bone tumour and cause night pain, but a firm palpable soft tissue mass with weight loss is not explained by it, and treating blind delays a time critical diagnosis. Antibiotics before imaging and tissue diagnosis also confound interpretation. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Perform an open biopsy of the thigh mass in the local hospital to obtain a tissue diagnosis promptly
options.rationale: Biopsy of a suspected primary bone sarcoma is planned and performed by the unit that will carry out the definitive resection, because a poorly placed tract contaminates compartments and can convert a limb sparing operation into an amputation. Speed matters but so does who holds the scalpel. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

options.text: Arrange plain radiographs of the femur and knee with prompt paediatric orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Night pain, pain persisting despite rest, weight loss and a firm deep mass over the distal femur are red flags for primary bone malignancy, and plain radiography is the first imaging test and is highly informative in osteosarcoma. Referral runs in parallel because biopsy must be planned by the treating sarcoma unit rather than performed locally. (Source: RCH CPG: Bone tumours)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in an adolescent athlete is usually benign and most often traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity or patellofemoral pain, both of which improve with relative rest and loading programmes. The features that break this pattern are pain that wakes the child at night, pain that worsens despite rest, systemic features such as weight loss, and any palpable deep mass, and osteosarcoma has a peak incidence in the adolescent growth spurt with the distal femur the commonest site. A raised alkaline phosphatase in this setting is supportive but not diagnostic and is not required to act. Plain radiography is the correct first investigation and typically demonstrates an aggressive periosteal reaction and abnormal matrix, after which magnetic resonance imaging stages the lesion locally. The biopsy must be arranged by the sarcoma service, since an inappropriately placed tract can compromise limb salvage.
key_points: Night pain and pain worsening despite rest are the cardinal red flags in adolescent bone pain
Tenderness above rather than at the tibial tuberosity moves the diagnosis away from apophysitis
Distal femur is the commonest osteosarcoma site and the peak is the adolescent growth spurt
Plain radiograph is the first imaging test; magnetic resonance imaging then stages locally
Biopsy is planned and performed by the sarcoma unit, never locally
explanation.pearls: A previous benign label such as growing pain or apophysitis is one of the strongest contributors to delayed sarcoma diagnosis, so treat failure to improve after six weeks of genuine rest as an indication to image rather than as a reason to reinforce the original advice.
